title: GOD TOLD ABIMELECH, “I KEPT YOU FROM SINNING AGAINST ME”
paragraphs: GOD TOLD ABIMELECH, “I KEPT YOU FROM SINNING AGAINST ME”
What if some of the sins you never committed were not proof of how strong you were—but evidence of how merciful God had been when you never even knew He was protecting you?
There is a sentence in Genesis that should make every believer sit still for a moment.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
Because once you understand it, you may never look at your own past the same way again.
God said to Abimelech:
“I kept you from sinning against Me.”
Genesis 20:6.
Read those words again.
Slowly.
I kept you.
There are sins you remember committing.
There are nights you wish you could erase.
There are words you would give almost anything to take back.
There are decisions that still make your stomach tighten when your mind wanders too far into yesterday.
You know the shame of what you did.
But have you ever thanked God for what you almost did?
For the relationship that collapsed before it could destroy you.
For the opportunity that mysteriously disappeared.
For the door you were furious God would not open.
For the person who stopped answering.
For the plan that failed.
For the temptation that somehow lost its opportunity.
For the night circumstances changed.
For the moment something inside you suddenly screamed, Don’t.
What if some of the interruptions you called bad luck were actually mercy?
What if some of your disappointments were restraints?
What if Heaven has rescued you from sins you never even realized you were about to commit?
That is part of what makes Genesis 20 so unsettling.
Abraham—the man of faith, the man carrying God's covenant promise—entered Gerar and became afraid.
Sarah was his wife.
But Abraham said of her, “She is my sister.”
Technically, there was a family relationship behind Abraham's statement, as Abraham later explained in Genesis 20:12. But he concealed the crucial truth that Sarah was also his wife.
And Abimelech, king of Gerar, took Sarah.
Then God entered the story.
Not quietly.
Not ambiguously.
God came to Abimelech in a dream and confronted him over another man's wife.
Abimelech protested that he had acted without knowing the full truth. And then comes the astonishing response of God:
“Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.”
The Hebrew makes the force of the statement unmistakable.
וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִי אֹתְךָ מֵחֲטֹו־לִי
Va'echsokh gam-anokhi otkha mechat'o-li.
In straightforward sense:
“And I also withheld you from sinning against Me.”
The verb וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ — va'echsokh carries the idea of withholding or restraining.
And מֵחֲטֹו־לִי — mechat'o-li means “from sinning against Me.”
God did not merely say, “You happened to make the right decision.”
He said, in effect:
I restrained you.
Then God explains the practical result:
“I did not let you touch her.”
That changes something.
Because we love testimonies about the grace that forgave us after we fell.
And we should.
The Gospel is gloriously about sinners being forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, redeemed, and made new through Jesus Christ.
But there is another kind of mercy we rarely talk about.
Preventing mercy.
Mercy that does not merely pull you out of the pit.
Mercy that sometimes keeps you from falling into it.
Think about your life.
Really think.
How many times have you credited yourself for victories that may have contained far more divine mercy than you realized?
“I would never do that.”
Be careful.
Peter once sounded certain too.
“Even if everyone else falls away…”
Not Peter.
He was sure of himself.
Then came the courtyard.
Then came the questions.
Then came the denials.
Then came the rooster.
And suddenly the man who believed himself incapable of abandoning Jesus discovered what fear could uncover inside him.
That is one reason Genesis 20:6 is so humbling.
It destroys the fantasy that the only thing separating us from catastrophic sin is superior character.
Yes, human choices matter.
Yes, Scripture commands self-control, holiness, vigilance, obedience, fleeing temptation, resisting the devil, renewing our minds, and putting sin to death.
Genesis 20:6 does not erase human responsibility.
But it reveals something else alongside it:
God can intervene.
God can restrain.
God can close a door.
God can interrupt circumstances.
God can prevent an action from reaching completion.
Abimelech had not touched Sarah because God had not permitted him to do so.
And perhaps that should change the way we tell our stories.
Maybe instead of saying only,
“I was strong enough to walk away,”
sometimes we should whisper,
“God, thank You for giving me the strength to leave.”
Instead of,
“I knew better,”
perhaps,
“Lord, thank You for reminding me of what I knew before desire made me forget.”
Instead of,
“I would never become that person,”
perhaps,
“Jesus, keep my heart close to You, because apart from Your grace I dare not trust myself.”
There is something terrifying about discovering what human beings are capable of.
But there is something breathtaking about discovering how relentlessly merciful God can be.
Somebody reading this remembers a door that closed.
You cried over it.
You prayed for God to reopen it.
You wondered why He seemed silent.
Maybe you watched somebody else receive what you wanted and secretly wondered whether God had forgotten you.
Years later, you discovered what was behind that door.
And suddenly your unanswered prayer looked different.
The rejection became protection.
The delay became mercy.
The “no” became rescue.
Not every disappointment means God was specifically preventing a particular sin. Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every inconvenience as a secret divine intervention.
But Genesis 20 gives us permission to recognize something equally important:
Sometimes God really does restrain people from sin.
And because we cannot see every movement of providence, there may be mercies in our histories whose names we will not know this side of eternity.
Imagine discovering in Heaven how many times God protected you when you thought nothing was happening.
How many temptations never reached you.
How many circumstances were rearranged.
How many disasters were interrupted.
How many times the Spirit convicted you before one more decision changed everything.
How many times Scripture returned to your memory at exactly the right moment.
How many times a brother or sister called when you were about to collapse.
How many times exposure frightened you back toward wisdom.
How many times God provided an escape from temptation and you barely recognized the exit.
You remember the scars.
God remembers the cliffs He kept you from reaching.
But there is another detail in Genesis 20 that cannot be missed.
God says Abimelech would have been sinning against Him.
Not merely against Abraham.
Not merely against Sarah.
Against God.
That is the seriousness of sin.
David understood this after his own horrifying moral collapse. His sin devastated real human beings, yet in Psalm 51 he recognized that ultimately his rebellion was against God.
Sin is not merely breaking an impersonal rule.
It is rebellion against the holy God who made us.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to becoming nicer people.
Our deepest problem requires more than improvement.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need Christ.
Because eventually every one of us reaches the place where the testimony cannot be:
“God kept me from every sin.”
He didn't.
Look at your own history.
Neither did you.
Neither did I.
There are lines we crossed.
Things we actually said.
Things we actually watched.
Things we actually desired.
People we actually wounded.
Lies we actually told.
Secrets we actually kept.
Moments when God provided a way out and we chose the temptation anyway.
And this is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
Because the God who can restrain sinners before they fall is also the God who can redeem sinners after they fall.
That road leads us to Jesus.
At the cross, Christ did not die for imaginary sinners.
He died for the guilty.
The ashamed.
The exposed.
The religious hypocrite.
The sexually broken.
The angry.
The addicted.
The greedy.
The self-righteous.
The liar.
The person whose secret would horrify everyone who thinks they know them.
Jesus did not wait for humanity to become respectable.
Christ came for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Christian Gospel is not that good people managed to climb high enough to reach God.
It is that God came down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
And maybe that is why this verse hits so deeply.
There are two testimonies of grace.
“God kept me from it.”
And:
“God rescued me after I did it.”
Both leave us with empty hands.
Neither allows boasting.
The first says, “I stood because God was merciful.”
The second says, “I fell, but Christ was merciful.”
Either way…
grace gets the final word.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you are not thinking about a sin God prevented.
You are thinking about one He didn't.
You did it.
You crossed the line.
You became the person you swore you would never become.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that your worst chapter disqualified you from ever having a beautiful ending.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin wasn't serious.
Grace does something far more powerful.
Grace tells you that Jesus is greater.
Repentance is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Repentance turns from sin and runs toward the Savior.
Confession brings darkness into light.
And the blood of Jesus does what your shame never could.
It cleanses.
You do not need to rewrite your history to be redeemed.
You need Jesus to rewrite what your history means.
The betrayal can become the place where repentance began.
The addiction can become the battlefield where dependence on Christ became real.
The failure can become the grave where pride finally died.
The exposed secret can become the moment hiding ended.
The broken years can become a testimony that screams:
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
This is why we say:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the cross means your sin does not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Jesus does.
So perhaps your prayer tonight should not merely be:
“God, forgive me for what I have done.”
Pray that.
But maybe add something you have rarely prayed:
“Father, thank You for the sins You kept me from committing.”
“Thank You for doors You closed.”
“Thank You for convictions I almost ignored.”
“Thank You for people You sent.”
“Thank You for exposing what needed exposure.”
“Thank You for interruptions I resented.”
“Thank You for every escape from temptation I recognized—and every one I never knew You provided.”
“And Lord… please keep me again.”
Because maturity is not reaching the point where you no longer need grace.
Maturity is realizing how desperately you have always needed it.
Be honest.
Somebody reading may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be final.
Do not let shame convince you that silence is holiness.
Sometimes another wounded believer needs to hear:
“I've been there too. And Jesus met me there.”
Come back and remember:
You are never too mature to pray, “Lord, keep me.”

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too. Sometimes one Scripture appearing on someone's screen at the right moment can begin a conversation that eternity remembers.

Scripture gives real warrant for materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel. But Scripture is equally clear that Christian giving must not be manipulated: each believer should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
It cannot purchase blessing.
It cannot purchase salvation.
It does not replace obedience, membership in a faithful local church, or whatever giving before God your conscience and biblical convictions lead you to practice.
If you want to glorify God through generosity toward Gospel work, this is one practical opportunity to participate.
Pray.
Follow.
Invite someone else to encounter the Gospel.
Because ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing an audience to Jesus.
And perhaps somewhere tonight, someone is seconds away from making a decision they will regret for years.
Maybe God will use a Scripture.
A conviction.
A phone call.
A closed door.
A Christian friend.
Even an article someone cared enough to share.
And years from now, that person may finally understand:
“That interruption wasn't God ruining my life.
That was God protecting it.”
Never forget this:
Some of the greatest testimonies of grace may be stories you will never be able to tell—because God, in His mercy, never let the story happen.
